query: For titanium alloys used as structural materials, formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could increase surface hardness and wear resistance. Specify the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to the untreated alloy, the service or test conditions under which the effect should hold, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a controlled experiment with clear results that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Plasma cladding a thin composite surface layer containing tungsten carbide (WC) particles onto a titanium alloy will increase its surface hardness and wear resistance relative to the untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventional titanium alloy with an unmodified, relatively soft and ductile surface microstructure that lacks hard, wear‐resistant phases.
generation.intervention: Apply a WC-reinforced composite coating onto the titanium alloy surface using plasma cladding. The coating is designed to incorporate well-dispersed WC particles in a metallic matrix (which may be based on titanium or a compatible alloy system) that bonds strongly with the substrate.
generation.conditions: The intervention is expected to improve performance under simulated industrial sliding wear conditions (e.g., dry and lubricated sliding tests at moderate speeds and loads) similar to those used in established wear studies.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a surface layer in which hard WC particles are anchored within a fine-grained metallic matrix. This composite microstructure creates a nailing effect that limits grain growth and acts as barriers to abrasive and adhesive wear.
generation.mechanism: WC particles, with their very high intrinsic hardness, act as micro-scale reinforcements that resist penetration and deformation during wear. Their presence in the cladded layer increases the overall surface hardness and diminishes the propagation of microcracks, thereby reducing abrasive removal. The metallic matrix, adapted to achieve reliable interfacial bonding with the titanium substrate, helps spread applied loads and maintains coating integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in surface hardness by an estimated 50% or more and a significant reduction in wear rate (potentially at least a 50% reduction) compared with the untreated titanium alloy under identical sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: Untreated titanium alloy with standard hardness and wear rate values typical for its composition and processing history.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only in the engineered surface layer. Under conditions where the coating might delaminate (e.g., high-temperature exposure or severe corrosive environments) or if the coating thickness is insufficient, the improvement may not persist.
generation.uncertainty: Exact improvement percentages depend on processing parameters (e.g., particle loading, cladding parameters) and testing conditions. Further optimization might be necessary to obtain the predicted enhancements.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of titanium alloy test samples, half with the WC-reinforced composite coating applied via plasma cladding and half left untreated. Subject all samples to standardized sliding wear tests, performed under both dry and lubricated conditions, while ensuring similar contact pressures, speeds, and distances.
measurements: Vickers or Rockwell surface hardness measurements across the cladded layer
Wear rate determination (e.g., measured in mm³·N⁻¹·m⁻¹)
SEM characterization of the surface microstructure and coating adherence
Evaluation of coating integrity (adhesion tests) after wear exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the WC-coated titanium samples do not exhibit at least a 30% improvement in surface hardness and a corresponding reduction in wear rate (at least a 30% decrease) compared to the untreated samples under identical test conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 5 and Figure 6 show illustrative results of the measurements of the wear rate on the friction paths for Al alloy and vanadium alloy, respectively. In the analyzed case, the tests were conducted under identical parameters for both materials. Therefore, linear wear, represented by the depth of the groove (friction track) in the radial section, was used for comparison. Friction tests were conducted under identical conditions for both alloys. With a sliding speed of 0.1 m/s and a time of 1800 s, the friction path was 180 m, which, with a friction radius of 3 mm, results in approx. 9550 friction cycles. A comparison of the width of the friction paths in Figure 5 and Figure 6 shows that the friction trace is much narrower for the vanadium alloy. The groove depth was measured on a measuring microscope. The results of the tests are summarized in Figure 7 along with the materials’ hardness measurements. The addition of vanadium resulted in an increase in the hardness of the alloy by 33% and a significant decrease in friction wear value by 73%.

The ceramic particle of WC is one of the most used hard phases due to its excellent properties [,]. WC is tungsten carbide which is a compound composed of tungsten and carbon with structure of hexagonal crystal. The hardness of WC is between 16 GPa and 22 GPa []. The wettability of WC with metal matrix is good. The hardening effect of WC on matrix is remarkable. On the other hand, the nailing effect produced by hard particles can limit grain growth and promote the hardness of metal matrix []. A coating of HEA reinforced with WC was prepared by plasma cladding to increase wear resistance []. The effect of WC content on microstructure and mechanical properties of composite coatings was analyzed. The results show that the existence of WC particles can effectively alleviate the wear damage of the coating and then significantly improve the wear-resistant properties of the coating. Although the addition of ceramic particles leads to an improvement of HEAs’ mechanical properties [,], the action mechanism of ceramic particles on microstructure and properties of HEAs is still not completely clear.
